newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Sturdier yen, weaker dollar to greet euro.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sturdier yen, weaker dollar to greet euro.

text.p: Markets may not know how the new euro currency will shape up, but they have already formed some assumptions about its rivals.

When the single European currency makes its scheduled debut on January 1, 1999, it will be pitted against a dollar and British pound that are weaker and a yen that is stronger than they are now, analysts say.

With the U.S. and British economies expected to be slowing by the time European economic and monetary union (EMU) is launched in 1999, the dollar and pound should be treading similar downward paths against the mark and yen because the German and Japanese economies are expected to be swinging upwards.

"We'll get the dollar growing stronger (on economic fundamentals)," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS in London. "Then there should be a cyclical improvement in European economies which will take the dollar off its highs, and 18 months down the road we'll probably be back where we are now."
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised its key federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent in March, its first such tightening in two years.
A stream of mainly healthy economic data since then has made the market envisage more rate hikes, but analysts see this tightening cycle petering out by the end of 1998.

"Over the course of 1998, the U.S. interest rate cycle will mature and start to go in the other direction. The dollar should peak out and we'll probably see some reversal in the latter half of 1998," said Ron Leven, global currency strategist at J.P. Morgan in New York.
Other U.S. analysts appeared to have similar views.

A recent Reuters survey of U.S. analysts showed average forecasts for a dollar in 1999 nearly 12 pfennigs lower than its recent July peaks above 1.80 marks, and seven yen below recent levels around 116 yen.
Concerns that EMU will be a broad-based grouping and hence have a single currency with watered-down strength will be dollar-supportive, they said.
But dollar gains on such speculation were expected to be limited, since such perceptions had dawned on the market long ago and were already being factored in.

"The question is at what point do (concerns about EMU) get fully priced into the dollar and it's probably not very far away. It's doing so already and certainly by 1.90 you've got a dollar that's pretty much priced in a weak euro scenario," Leven said.
REVERSAL OF FORTUNES
The yen, meanwhile, is expected to gain the upper hand in general.
By the time Europe's single currency becomes reality, the currently sketchy signs of recovery in Japan's economy are expected to have become more concrete.

And since the Bank of Japan has kept its official discount rate at its lowest-ever 0.5 percent, which is also the lowest in the world, for nearly two years, analysts say Japanese rates have no way to go but up.
The outlook was not so clear-cut for sterling, which, second to the euro, will become the European currency with the biggest market once EMU is launched.

Pulling sterling lower around the euro kick-off will be the state of Britain's economy. Right now it is ebullient, with many in the market judging that only tighter interest rates will be able to keep the economy from spinning out of control.
Speculation of a rise in key rates soon have drawn punters to the pound, with sterling shooting to its highest in six years against the mark this week.
At 6.75 percent, the British base lending rate is already higher than any of its major European counterparts with the exception of Ireland and Greece.
But all this, as in the case of the U.S. and its dollar, will likely lose steam over the next 18 months, analysts said.

"We should see Britain's interest rate cycle peaking out, and people will be looking for the turn in the rate cycle and be contrasting it to the cycle in the continental European economies. So that should cap sterling's strength and make it retrace," said UBS's Lambert.
THE BENEFITS OF BEING AN OUTSIDER

On the plus side is the charm of Britain as Europe's safe haven amid the uncertainty shrouding EMU, since Britain has all but decided to stay out of at least the first round of monetary union. This perception has also added fuel to the pound's recent rally against the mark.

Sterling is expected to bask in its safe-haven status as long as markets are unsure about factors ruling the euro's stability, such as which countries will be members and the degree of hawkishness in the European Central Bank's monetary policy.

"Until the euro is established and the ECB has proved its mettle, it will continue to be dogged by a credibility problem that will lessen any cyclical improvement in the mark and other currencies," said Andrew Snowball, treasury economist at the Cooperative Bank here.
Snowball said sterling would also benefit from different views among European states on what shape EMU should take: "That sort of uncertainty will definitely support (sterling)."
But once the uncertainty about EMU is over the economic fundamentals are likely to come to the fore, pushing the pound lower against the continental currencies.

"The UK will be seen as an economy that's growing too fast, has a trade disequilibrium, and an inflation problem, whereas I think the main euro countries will still have a lot of spare capacity and a very low inflation rate," said John Calverley, chief economist at American Express Bank in London.
